title: Journeys east and a new town
hook: Guru Tegh Bahadur travels as far as Assam and founds the town that becomes Anandpur

segments.voice: Yesterday, twenty-two claimants at Bakala, and Makhan Shah, the trader shouting from the roof. Your line was the guru is found.

Two suitcases and a rented shop in a new country. A cheap old house, fixed up one room at a time after a hard year. Starting over takes a kind of courage that isn't loud at all. Guru Tegh Bahadur, the new ninth Guru, did not have an easy welcome. Some of the disappointed claimants turned hostile; tradition says one of them even had a shot fired at him. So the quiet Guru did two things. He built a new home, and he set out on a long road east.
screen: `SOMEONE WHO STARTED OVER.` → `NOT AN EASY WELCOME.` → `A NEW HOME, AND THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: First, the town. In 1665 the Guru bought land in the Shivalik foothills, near Kiratpur, from the ruling family of the hill state of Kahlur. He named the settlement Chakk Nanaki, after his mother, Mata Nanaki. It was rough ground by the river Sutlej, with hills behind. Over the years it would grow into a Sikh center known as Anandpur, the city of bliss. You met the word anand on day fifty-three, in the song of bliss. Much of the rest of this camp happens there. Second, the journey. Soon after founding the town, the Guru set out east, the way Guru Nanak had gone long before, visiting Sikh communities and holy places. He traveled through Agra and Allahabad, to Benares, and on to Patna, on the Ganges. There he left his wife, Mata Gujri, who was expecting a child, and kept going: to Dhaka, in Bengal, and all the way to Assam, in the far east, where tradition says he helped make peace between an imperial army and the Assamese kingdom. While he was far away, his son was born in Patna. The Guru would not see him for years. The quiet man from the room below ground didn't wait for a perfect life. He took rough land and started a town. He took the road and strengthened scattered communities. Build where you are, with what you have, and let it grow into something you may never fully see.
screen: `CHAKK NANAKI, 1665.` · `ANANDPUR, THE CITY OF BLISS.` · `EAST AS FAR AS ASSAM.` · `A SON BORN IN PATNA.` · then, large: `BUILD WHERE YOU ARE.`

segments.voice: Think of something you've wanted to begin but keep saving for when life is calmer: a habit, a project, a friendship, a garden. Picture the rough ground as it is now, not ideal, and the first small stake you could put in it. If a seed, a pot or a notebook is near, you can even make that start now; if not, just hold the beginning.
Anandpur. The city of bliss that grew from Chakk Nanaki, the town Guru Tegh Bahadur founded near Kiratpur before journeying east as far as Assam.
Your line: build where you are. Rough ground was enough for a town. Day seventy-six.

howItsDone: Sikhs visit Anandpur Sahib, the town founded by Guru Tegh Bahadur, and gurdwaras mark his travels in the east, from Patna and Dhaka to Dhubri in Assam.

original.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi: anand, bliss; pur, town. The city of bliss.

trapdoor: what you thought: a Guru moved house and went traveling.
what it means: starting over on rough ground, and strengthening scattered communities, without waiting for a perfect life.
what a scholar hears: Chakk Nanaki was founded in 1665 on land from the Raja of Kahlur (Bilaspur); the name Anandpur came into use later.

notes: The shot fired at the Guru is traditionally attributed to Dhir Mal's men (Shihan); left unnamed. Confirm.
Chakk Nanaki founded 1665 on land bought from the Raja of Kahlur (Bilaspur); confirm. The date the name Anandpur came into use is debated; stated as 'later'.
Assumes 'anand' was taught on day 53 (The song of bliss). Confirm.
Assam: tradition says he accompanied Raja Ram Singh's campaign and helped make peace with the Ahom kingdom (Dhubri). Confirm phrasing.
Order of the journey (Agra, Allahabad, Benares, Patna, Dhaka, Assam) simplified; confirm.
